reason: The candidate gets both key points right: you can find out who accessed your personal electronic health data, and that information must stay available for at least three years from each access. Passage [1] supports both points. The wording is weak, though. It says the passage "does not specify exactly how long" and then gives the three-year minimum. It also mentions the "duration of such access", but the passage only lists the date and time of access. Compared with the reference, it leaves out that the information is free of charge, is provided without delay through the electronic health data access services, and can come as automatic notifications. These are flaws, but they do not contradict the reference or the passages.

The answer correctly says people can authorise relatives or other close persons to access their data. But it wrongly says the passages do not give a duration. Passage [3] states the authorisation can be for a limited or unlimited period, and if needed for a specific purpose only. So half of the question goes unanswered, and the answer misdescribes what was retrieved. It also misses that this happens through proxy services that let people manage their authorisations. Calling the authorised people 'close friends' is a small stretch of the passages' wording, 'close natural persons'.

The candidate answer is wrong on the main point. It says it cannot give a maximum validity, but the reference answer sets it at 10 years. It also leaves out that the permit can be extended only once, for up to another 10 years, with justification given one month before it expires. It is still faithful to the passages. They contain no maximum duration. Passage [2] supports its claims about extension: that it requires an amendment, may carry an extra fee, and can be used for reviewers or further analysis.

The first part of the answer is right: you can add data to your EHR, and that data must be clearly distinguishable from data entered by professionals. But it then concludes that clinicians may not recognise the data as coming from the patient unless someone tells them. That contradicts both the reference and passage [2]. The whole point of the 'clearly distinguishable' requirement is that clinicians can see the data was entered by the patient. The answer also leaves out that patients cannot change data entered by health professionals. Passage [1] states this, and the reference includes it. The final sentence has no support in the passages.

The candidate says the GDPR does not apply to deceased persons' data and that Member States may set their own rules. That matches the reference answer. Both points are supported directly by Recital 27 in passage [1].

The candidate answers the question's core point: the Commission reports to the European Parliament and Council every four years, as Article 97(1) GDPR in passage [4] states. It leaves out the first deadline of 25 May 2020 and that the reports must be made public. Those are minor gaps, not errors. Everything it says is supported by the retrieved passage.

The candidate correctly says that the EHDS defines personal electronic health data as data concerning health and genetic data processed in electronic form. It also gives the GDPR definition of 'data concerning health' accurately, which matches the reference answer. The extra point about non-personal electronic health data is backed by passage [4], and the GDPR definition is backed by passage [2]. It does not say outright that the EHDS takes over the GDPR definitions by reference (passage [3]); it says the two "align" instead. That is a weaker way to describe the link, but it is not wrong. The final sentence is somewhat vague but does not contradict the sources.

The candidate gets the basic "yes" right but makes two errors. First, it bases the delay on Article 8 and says natural persons can restrict access. The power actually belongs to Member States, which can delay a patient's access on patient-safety and ethical grounds (passage 7). Article 8 is about patients themselves restricting what health professionals can see. Second, it names GDPR Article 21 as the relevant rule and calls it a "right to restrict processing." Article 21 is the right to object; the right to restrict processing is Article 18. The right answer is Article 23, which lets legislative measures restrict data subject rights when necessary and proportionate. The candidate never mentions Article 23. The passages do not support linking this delay to Article 8 or Article 21, so the answer is not faithful to them.

The candidate says there is no information on whether a non-EU research institute can apply for EHDS data. That is wrong: passage [9] gives the eligibility conditions for third-country applicants. The country must either be an authorised participant with a national contact point for secondary use, or let Union applicants access its data on conditions no more restrictive than the EHDS. The candidate also gets the GDPR principle wrong. It names "necessity and proportionality", but the governing rule is that a transfer may happen only if the conditions of Chapter V are met (see passages [4] and [6]). Nothing in the passages supports the "necessity and proportionality" claim. Its mention of adequacy decisions under Article 45 has some support, but it is incomplete and it is framed as an exception to the wrong principle.

The candidate gets the main mechanisms right: researchers find datasets through the dataset catalogue, and a data quality and utility label documents quality. Its claims are supported by passages [9] and [10]. It is incomplete in three ways. It does not say the catalogue is standardised and machine-readable. It leaves out the per-dataset metadata (source, nature, access conditions), even though passage [1] covers it. It also omits that a label is mandatory for datasets funded with public Union or national money. Nothing it states contradicts the reference or goes beyond the passages.

The question has two parts, and the candidate answers only one. On who pays, it correctly says that each controller can be held liable for the entire damage, and that compensation may be split by responsibility when they are joined in the same proceedings, as long as the data subject gets full and effective compensation. That part is supported by passage [2]. It never answers which company the data subject turns to for their rights. The key point is that the data subject can exercise their rights against each joint controller, whatever their internal arrangement says, and the answer leaves this out. It also never uses the term "joint controllers". The claims it does make come from the passages, so it is faithful, but it is incomplete on a central part of the question.
